newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain - full text of stability statement.
newsitem.headline: Spain - full text of stability statement.

text.p: Following is the full text of the Spanish government's projections and plans to ensure fiscal stability into the year 2000.

1. During the course of 1996, the Spanish economy has modified the deceleration that it had been experiencing since the middle of 1995. This change stems principally from the correction of macroeconomic desequilibriums, which, at the same time, have allowed the economy to progress on the path to convergence. The guidelines of economic policy have focused on containing public expenditure and on the reform of markets which has given rise to greater macroeconomic stability, reflected in the sharp reduction in inflation and in real interest rates.

2. In 1997 there will be an additional correction in inflation and in the public deficit, in line with the convergence criteria, which will permit an improvement in the expectations of economic agents and a comfortable financial economic situation characterised by a context of low interest rates which will help raise the rythym of economic growth to three percent. At the same time, the healthier macroeconomic situation and continued structural reforms will allow more intensive employement creation than in 1996.

3. The outlook for the economic cycle suggests average growth of 3.2 percent between 1997 and the year 2000 and average inflation in terms of the private consumption deflator of 2.3 percent. Therefore, we foresee a more moderate evolution with healthier, more sustained growth that creates more jobs than in previous cycles. Real growth is seen above inflation in each of the years. This new pattern of Spanish economic growth is the result of a context of greater macroeconomic stability, the ongoing flexibilisation of markets for products and factors our monetary integration with countries of traditional monetary stability."

"4. Given this economic outlook, the budget projection reflects a continual fall in the deficit of public administrations in terms of GDP from three percent in 1997 to 1.6 percent in 2000. Even in the most unfavourable situation in terms of expected growth, the public deficit would be systematically below three percent of GDP. Fiscal consolidation efforts are focused on restraining current expenditures, whose portion of GDP will be reduced by two percentage points during the reference period. Therefore despite the reduction of fiscal pressure and the increase of investment expenditure there will be a primary surplus, tending clearly higher, of public administrations each year.

A restraining of the public deficit and the growth just detailed will lead to a continual reduction since 1996 of the debt burden by more than four percentage points to a level near 65 percent of GDP in the year 2000.
